title: why five times
hook: why five times; standing, bowing, forehead to the ground

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five pillars, a house built on five. Today, the second pillar, up close. Day ten.
screen: `THE FIVE PILLARS — A HOUSE BUILT ON FIVE.` → `DAY 10.`

segments.voice: Ten past one on a weekday, in the stockroom behind a hardware store. One of the staff flattens a clean cardboard box on the floor, turns to face a particular direction, and stands very still. Then he bows, hands on his knees. Then he goes all the way down, forehead to the cardboard, between the paint cans and the delivery crates. A few minutes later he folds the box away and goes back to the register. Why five times a day? And why the whole body?
screen: `A STOCKROOM, JUST AFTER ONE.` → `FOREHEAD TO THE FLOOR.` → `WHY FIVE? WHY THE BODY?`

segments.voice: Salat. It's the second pillar, and it isn't quite what English means by prayer. Du'a is asking, in your own words, any time. Salat is a set shape, at set times, with set words. The Qur'an says: “Lo! worship preserveth from lewdness and iniquity.” The five times follow the sun. Fajr before sunrise. Dhuhr after midday. Asr in the afternoon. Maghrib just after sunset. Isha at night. Where does five come from? A saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tells it. On the Night Journey he was given fifty daily prayers. On the way back, Musa, Moses, asked what he'd been given, and said: your people can't manage that; go back and ask for less. He went back, again and again, until it was five. And God said: five, with the reward of fifty. Many pray them at five separate times; Shia practice also allows joining them into three sittings, and the prayers are still five. Now the body. Each prayer is made of units called rak'ahs, and each moves through the same shapes. Standing, and reciting al-Fatiha, the seven verses from day two. Bowing, back flat, hands on the knees. Standing again. Then sujud: forehead, nose, palms, knees and toes on the ground. Another saying tells that a person is never nearer to God than there. The part of you that thinks, set down where your feet were.
screen: `SALAT — A SET SHAPE, AT SET TIMES.` · `FIVE TIMES, FOLLOWING THE SUN.` · `FIFTY, THEN FIVE.` · `STANDING, BOWING, FOREHEAD DOWN.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand for a moment, then bow a little, hands on your knees, and notice how your breath changes in each shape. If you'd rather stay seated, lower your head toward your chest, slowly, and feel what the body says when it bows. Stay there, and let the body do the praying for once, without any words.
Salat. The prayer in its set shape: five times a day, standing, bowing, forehead to the ground. Tenth word.
Your line: the body prays too. And if you prayed for a while and then stopped, you're in plenty of company: many come back one prayer at a time. Day ten.

howItsDone: Muslims pray salat five times a day, facing Mecca, in a set sequence of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting; they may pray at home, at work, at a mosque, or anywhere clean.

original.note: Arabic: the set prayer, the second pillar. often spoken as salah.

trapdoor: what you thought: prayer is talking to God in words.
what it means: salat — a set prayer at five set times, made of standing, bowing and putting the forehead on the ground.
what a scholar hears: salat, distinct from du'a; five from fifty on the Night Journey (Bukhari); and sujud, where a hadith in Muslim says a person is never nearer to God.

Worded as what people do, not a ruling (the five prayers stay five); confirm a Keeper is comfortable with it.
Pickthall 29:45 quoted from memory: '...and establish worship. Lo! worship preserveth from lewdness and iniquity, but verily remembrance of Allah is more important.' Confirm.
Night Journey hadith (Bukhari 349, also 3207; Muslim 162): fifty reduced to five at Musa's urging, 'five, and they are fifty' in reward. Paraphrased; confirm numbers.
Joining prayers: 'many pray them at five separate times; Shia practice also allows joining them into three sittings'. Sunni schools also allow combining when traveling. Confirm phrasing.
Sujud: the seven body parts (forehead with nose, two palms, two knees, two feet's toes) per Bukhari 812. Confirm.
